I am 62 years old, and I have been farming this land in Quzhou since I was a young girl. My husband passed away five years ago, and now my son helps me with the heavy machinery work when he is not working in the county town, but I make all the decisions myself. I have about 7 mu of good flat land that I farm, and I know every plot. I finished middle school, so I can read the seed bags and fertilizer labels well enough, and I talk to the agro-shop owner in town to know what varieties are selling.

For me, there is really only one choice: I will plant **winter wheat followed by summer maize** in rotation on all 7 mu. This is what we have always done on the North China Plain, and it is the only system that gives us two crops a year and puts food on the table. Wheat prices have been steady, and maize is needed for the livestock feed market. I thought about cotton, but at my age I cannot manage the endless pesticide sprays and the hand-picking labor cotton demands. Wheat and maize are mechanized for sowing and harvest, which saves my back.

For **winter wheat**, I will sow in early October after rotary tillage. I use an improved wheat variety that the local shop recommends every year — it yields well and resists lodging. I will put down a basal compound fertilizer at sowing and topdress with urea in the spring when the wheat greens up. I irrigate four times: once before winter to protect the seedlings, once at green-up, once at jointing, and once at flowering. The well water is still good here. For pests, I spray insecticide twice, herbicide once, and fungicide once — the shop mixes the tanks for me now.

For **summer maize**, I plant immediately after the wheat harvest in early June. I use hybrid maize seed, Nongda 372 or something similar, one package per mu. I do not till for maize anymore — I plant no-till directly into the wheat stubble to save time, fuel, and labor. I give it less fertilizer than wheat because maize here grows fast in the summer heat. I irrigate twice, usually once after sowing if it is dry, and once at the big trumpet leaf stage. I spray insecticide twice and herbicide once. The combine harvester comes in October.

This is my plan.

decision.reasoning_summary: I am a 62-year-old woman farming 7 mu in Quzhou County on the North China Plain. Given my age and limited labor, I stick to the mechanized wheat-maize rotation system that is reliable and familiar. Wheat is sown in October with rotary tillage, irrigated four times, and fertilized heavily because it is our staple cash crop. Maize is no-till planted immediately after wheat harvest in June to save labor and time, receiving lighter inputs but still producing well. I avoid cotton because its labor and pesticide demands are too high for me to manage alone. This double-cropping system maximizes my small land area and provides stable income from two harvests per year.
